_comment: Demo verification + decision policies for the seeded tools.
Read this before trusting anything it produces:
The promote gate is a CHECK constraint precisely so no code path could
route around it, and that leaves one sharp gap —
the gate's evidence numbers are TYPED IN BY A HUMAN, because nothing in the
system counts shadow calls or labels false positives yet. This file types
them in. It is a DEV SEED and it is exactly that bypass, used
deliberately and in one place, so that the receipt has a
real ACTIVE policy to name instead of rendering 'no policy configured' for
every call.
It is not wired into any service. It runs only when a human runs
`yarn mcp:policies`, against a local database, and the approver is a
literal string that says so. Receipts turning verification_records into
counted shadow calls is what makes the gate mechanical; until then the
four-eyes rule is procedural and this file is the proof of that.
toolId values must match scripts/mcp/seed/catalogue.json.
The rules are deliberately weak — a temperature band and a freshness
window a healthy provider always clears. A demo seed that struck real
public providers on ordinary responses would be teaching the wrong lesson
about what the engine is for. To watch a FAIL, narrow `max` on the
temperature rule and call the tool.
Weights are not an even split. The stage scores passedWeight over
consideredWeight against passThreshold — see
src/modules/verification/domain/stages/deterministic-stage.ts — so a single
failing rule of weight w scores 1 − w, and at a 0.7 threshold a rule
weighted 0.30 or less can NEVER fail its policy on its own (0.30 lands on
0.70 exactly, and the comparison is >=). What a rule is worth is therefore
a judgement about how badly its violation ruins the answer: a stale price
condemns the call, a malformed logo URL does not. Each rule's _comment says
which side of that line it is on and why.

rules._comment: The recorded extremes on Earth, rounded outward. A band that fails an honest reading is a false positive, and this rule exists to catch a sensor returning 9999 or a unit mix-up, not to grade the weather.
Three hours. Forecast models publish hourly and a provider's clock may run fast; the five-minute future tolerance is skew, not a defect.

_comment: No length rule and no uniqueness rule, both on purpose.
Uniqueness is out because two genuinely different places share a name —
there are dozens of Springfields, and an honest upstream returning all of
them would be struck for telling the truth.
A length rule is out because 'no such place' is a legitimate answer.
Measured 2026-08-25: open-meteo signals it by omitting `results`
entirely, which the mapping already turns into a void rather than a
strike. Adding MIN_ARRAY_LENGTH here would buy nothing and put a whole
class of correct responses one mapping change away from a strike.

rules._comment: A match with no coordinates is not a geocode. This catches the upstream that returns a name row it could not resolve, and the mapping that silently drops a field after an upstream rename — the agent gets a place it cannot point at.

The whole planet, so no honest reading can fail it. It catches the coordinates swapped round — a longitude landing in the latitude field is out of band past 90 for most of the world — and a null coerced to a number.
The other half of the pair. Wide for the same reason: it exists to catch a projected metre value or a degrees-times-1e7 integer arriving where degrees were promised, not to grade the fix.

rules._comment: One is the floor, and an empty collection does not fail this rule at all — an unknown CoinGecko id is a legitimate empty answer and routes to the empty-result policy. Weighted low because the interesting failure here is a wrong price, not a short list.

A zero price is the failure that costs an agent money: it is what a missing field coerced to a number looks like, and an agent sizing a trade on it would size it infinite. The floor is a millionth of a cent so that the cheapest real memecoin still clears. No ceiling — a token can be worth anything.

Thirty minutes, not five: CoinGecko's free tier refreshes on its own schedule and lags, so a five-minute band would strike an honest provider for the upstream's cadence — exactly the false positive the engine exists to avoid. A price stale by half an hour is still a wrong answer to charge for, which is why this one is over the line. The five-minute future tolerance is clock skew, not a defect.

Deliberately below the line. A malformed logo URL does not make the price wrong, and no agent trades on an icon; failing the call for it would refund the caller and strike the provider over a broken image. Worth checking, not worth condemning — 0.10 can never fail this policy on its own.

One row per asset. A repeated id is the shape of a paginated fetch that looped, and it would make an agent summing market caps double-count — but the prices themselves are still right, so it warns rather than condemns.

rules._comment: A balance without the slot it was read at is unusable: the agent cannot tell a current reading from a cached one, and an RPC node that answered from behind a fork looks identical to one that did not.

No account has ever held less than nothing. A negative here means a signed-integer wrap or a subtraction the mapping did on its own, and an agent that reads it will conclude the payer cannot fund a transaction it could in fact fund. No ceiling: the supply grows.

A floor and no ceiling, because mainnet slots only ever rise — a ceiling written today becomes a false positive the week the chain passes it. The floor is far behind the live head and catches the answer that is not a mainnet slot at all: a devnet reading, a block height, a zero.

rules._comment: The extract and the page it came from. Without the source the agent cannot cite or re-fetch what it just read, and an extractor that followed a redirect to somewhere else is indistinguishable from one that did not.

Over the line here, unlike the logo URL on get_token_market, because this URL is the provenance of the text: an agent that quotes the extract cites this. A path fragment, an error string or an empty value leaves the quote unattributable.

Zero tokens is the failure this tool has: a 200 that carries a cookie wall, a JS shell or a boilerplate strip that took the article with it. The caller paid for text and received none, which is the clearest refund case in the catalogue.

rules._comment: A search that matches nothing is a real answer, not a defect, and an empty collection routes to the empty-result policy rather than failing here. The rule earns its place only against a collection that resolved to something unreadable, so it is weighted accordingly.
A result the agent cannot open is not a search result. The pageId is how it fetches the article; a row with a title and no id sends the agent back to a second search it already paid to avoid.

Over the line here, unlike the same rule on get_token_market, because the product of this tool IS the list: the same article repeated five times is a five-result response with one result in it, and the caller paid for breadth.

Deliberately below the line. An odd word count does not make a search result wrong — the title and the id are what the agent acts on — so a stub reported as -1 by a mis-parse should not refund the caller and strike the provider. At 0.20 it cannot fail this policy alone, by design.

_comment: The live demo's broken half. A byte-for-byte copy of search_wikipedia.default's four
rules, weights and threshold — copied rather than shared BECAUSE a policy is
resolved by tool (DecisionPolicyService.resolveForTraffic(toolId)), so a
second tool needs its own row or it judges nothing and settles UNVERIFIED.
Keep the weights identical to the original. The demo's whole claim is that
the SAME checks that pass on the healthy binding fail on this one, and a
policy tuned to make failing easier would be staging the result the page
exists to prove is real.
mode ACTIVE is load-bearing: effectiveConsequence() gives a SHADOW policy
the PASS consequence regardless of verdict, so a shadow copy here would
read 'FAIL, and charged anyway' on the page.
